story.headline: Lugano go nine clear in Super League
story.summary: Last week's brief had Lugano six points clear; the lead is now nine, and it widened on the very afternoon the chasing pack stumbled
story.display_body: Last week's brief had Lugano six points clear; the lead is now nine, and it widened on the very afternoon the chasing pack stumbled. Young Boys (YB, the Bern club that has dominated the league for years) lost 3–5 at home to FC Zürich, their first defeat of the season after conceding two late goals, and Lugano then beat Basel 2–1 in Ticino for their 11th win in 12 league games. SRF reports it is Lugano's 23rd match without defeat in all competitions, and describes Basel as dominating the ball (about 65 percent) without creating much: their only goal came from Philip Otele in the 37th minute. In the same round, reigning champions Thun beat bottom club Lausanne 5–4 after trailing 1–4 in the 70th minute.
story.why: nine points after 12 rounds is a big cushion, and the two clubs best placed to chase Lugano, YB and Basel, are both struggling right now.

story.headline: Arsenal win at Anfield, go three clear
story.summary: Kai Havertz scored in the first half and Arsenal then defended for their lives: Liverpool did not manage a single shot on target after the break, according to BBC Sport
story.display_body: Kai Havertz scored in the first half and Arsenal then defended for their lives: Liverpool did not manage a single shot on target after the break, according to BBC Sport. It is Arsenal's first Premier League win at Liverpool since 2012, and it came four days after a Carabao Cup (England's second-tier knockout cup) exit at League Two Fleetwood Town, which manager Mikel Arteta said had sharpened his players. The win leaves the reigning champions top with 24 points from nine games, three clear of Manchester City, with Liverpool fifth on 15.
story.why: a three-point lead after nine games is small, but beating a direct rival away from home, with the league's joint-best defence so far (five goals conceded, fewest in the table), is the sort of result title races turn on.

story.headline: Antonelli is youngest F1 world champion
story.summary: Kimi Antonelli, the Mercedes driver, clinched the 2026 drivers' title by finishing third behind winner Max Verstappen (Red Bull) and Lewis Hamilton (Ferrari)
story.display_body: Kimi Antonelli, the Mercedes driver, clinched the 2026 drivers' title by finishing third behind winner Max Verstappen (Red Bull) and Lewis Hamilton (Ferrari). He is 20 years and 68 days old, beating Sebastian Vettel's record as youngest champion by three years and 66 days, and is the first Italian champion since Alberto Ascari in 1953. He only needed to stay out of trouble: the title could only have gone elsewhere if his team-mate George Russell or Hamilton had won the race. He now leads Verstappen 380 points to 261, with races still to come this season. The race itself, per Autosport, was reshaped by a red flag after Valtteri Bottas's Cadillac hit the wall, which set up a short sprint to the finish that Verstappen held off Hamilton to win — his third victory in four races.
story.why: a driver who was still a teenager until late August has won the sport's biggest prize, and his team-mate Russell is fourth on 250 points.

story.headline: Hamilton wants Ferrari talks after Leclerc clash
story.summary: Hamilton started from pole but lost momentum on lap one when team-mate Charles Leclerc went past by cutting the grass at Turn 5; Verstappen took second
story.display_body: Hamilton started from pole but lost momentum on lap one when team-mate Charles Leclerc went past by cutting the grass at Turn 5; Verstappen took second. Stewards gave Leclerc only a five-second penalty, which Hamilton and Verstappen both called soft, and Hamilton, who said he was "pushed off by my own team-mate", ended up second, short of the win. He said after the race Ferrari "need serious talks". The fight for second in the championship is now tight: Verstappen 261, Hamilton 259, Russell 250 and Leclerc 245.
story.why: Ferrari have two stars and no clear order between them, and with the title gone, the remaining races decide who finishes best of the rest.

story.headline: Yamaha boycotts MotoGP Qatar round
story.summary: Yamaha announced its factory team and its satellite team Pramac will not travel to the Qatar Grand Prix on 6–8 November, citing the ongoing Middle East war and a clause in its employee contracts that lets it bar travel to war-affected regio
story.display_body: Yamaha announced its factory team and its satellite team Pramac will not travel to the Qatar Grand Prix on 6–8 November, citing the ongoing Middle East war and a clause in its employee contracts that lets it bar travel to war-affected regions. Autosport reports at least four riders will miss the race, the season's 20th round. It follows a week of riders pressing MotoGP to cancel or move the event; the same weekend, Marc Marquez won in Malaysia to close in on the title.
story.why: a manufacturer is skipping a race on safety and contract grounds, and Autosport is already asking what it means for Formula 1's Qatar and Abu Dhabi rounds.

story.headline: Vacherot wins Swiss Indoors in Basel
story.summary: Valentin Vacherot of Monaco (ATP 31) came back from a set down to beat Jiri Lehecka of the Czech Republic (ATP 21) 2–6, 6–3, 6–3
story.display_body: Valentin Vacherot of Monaco (ATP 31) came back from a set down to beat Jiri Lehecka of the Czech Republic (ATP 21) 2–6, 6–3, 6–3. It is only his second ATP tour title, a little over a year after his surprise win at the Shanghai Masters (a top-tier ATP 1000 event). In the doubles, the Swiss pair Henry Bernet and Dominic Stricker narrowly missed the title. SRF notes Lehecka, who dominated the first set, gave away the decisive break with two unforced errors on his own serve at 3–5.
story.why: Basel is the Swiss tennis calendar's marquee week; there was no Swiss singles finalist, but the doubles final came close.

story.headline: Zverev becomes world number one
story.summary: Alexander Zverev, 29, takes the top ranking for the first time, making him the oldest man to do so in more than 50 years, per BBC Sport
story.display_body: Alexander Zverev, 29, takes the top ranking for the first time, making him the oldest man to do so in more than 50 years, per BBC Sport. It rests on a breakthrough season: he won his first Grand Slams at the French Open (beating Flavio Cobolli in June) and the US Open, and lost the Wimbledon final to Jannik Sinner. BBC notes he has lost 10 straight matches against Sinner, so the ranking does not settle the big rivalries. The BBC piece also records that Zverev has denied past abuse allegations from two former partners; an ATP-commissioned investigation found "insufficient evidence", and a Berlin trial ended after a week with a settlement, not a verdict. Elsewhere, Carlos Alcaraz won the Vienna Open on Sunday 1 November, beating Alex de Minaur 6–1, 6–4.
story.why: the new number one is a two-time major champion this year, but the same report notes Sinner has beaten him ten times running.

story.headline: Iran offers two-day Hormuz reopening
story.summary: Iran said it could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days instead of seven if the US accepts its conditions, a day after Trump threatened a 'sledgehammer' blow.
story.display_body: Iran said on Monday 2 November that it could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days, rather than the seven days it had first proposed, if Washington accepts its conditions. The offer came a day after Donald Trump said the US would "at some point" have to hit Iran with a "sledgehammer" blow. Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei called the shorter timetable "a further sign of Iran's good faith" and said messages were still being passed through mediators. Qatar has held talks with both sides in Doha for several days. Trump made the threat at a campaign rally in Iowa on Sunday 1 November, two days before the midterm elections. He said the only reason he had "not yet finished with Iran" was that he wanted "to be nice". He also confirmed he had discussed Iran with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu; Axios reported the call covered the timing of renewed strikes. Tehran is hardening its own tone: Iranian media say two large tankers hit mines in the strait and are on fire and a third was struck by projectiles (not independently confirmed). Iran's parliament is also debating bills to leave the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.
story.why: Hormuz carries a large share of the world's seaborne oil and LNG (liquefied natural gas), and the closure is already pushing up European gas and power prices, including in Switzerland (see below). Whether Washington takes up the offer or resumes strikes after Tuesday's vote will set energy prices for the winter.

story.headline: Zelensky offers refinery truce for Patriots
story.summary: Zelensky said Ukraine would pause strikes on Russian refineries for a month if the US supplied Patriot interceptors for that month.
story.display_body: Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sunday 1 November that Ukraine would stop striking Russian oil refineries for a month if the US supplied Patriot interceptors for the same month. Trump has demanded that Kyiv and Moscow stop attacking each other's energy sites, as fuel prices drive up US inflation. Speaking on Fox News, Zelensky said Ukraine could not stop responding while Russia hits its power grid: "If you want us not to attack Russian refineries… give us Patriot missiles." On Friday 30 October the State Department approved a possible $2.1 billion sale of 500 PAC-3 MSE interceptors, paid for by Canada, Germany and Norway. Zelensky warned that deliveries could begin "only in a few years". He wants the missiles taken from existing US stocks now, with the new contracts used to replace them later. Ukraine's grid operator ordered emergency power cuts in Kyiv and the surrounding region on Monday.
story.why: Zelensky is offering a pause in strikes on Russian refineries, which have raised fuel prices, in return for the air defences Ukraine needs to protect its power grid this winter.

story.headline: Hackers send fake nuclear alerts in Ukraine
story.summary: Ukraine's Air Alert app sent fake nuclear and chemical warnings around Kyiv as the Oleshky truce ended; Russia reported similar hacks.
story.display_body: Ukraine's official Air Alert app sent fake warnings of nuclear and chemical threats around Kyiv shortly after 22:00 on Sunday 1 November, the same day a six-day local ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky ended. The fake messages also warned of street fighting and claimed Russia had fired its hypersonic Oreshnik missile. Ukraine's air force said the app "appears to have been subjected to enemy influence" and posted "There is no radiation threat!" Ukraine's Centre for Strategic Communications blamed Russia, pointing to Russian-language text in one of the messages. Russia in turn reported fake radiation alerts on its own warning apps. On Monday, Ukraine's General Staff accused Moscow of using the truce to rearm and rotate troops; the Kremlin called that "normal practice".
story.why: false alerts teach people to ignore real warnings, so hacking them puts civilians at risk as heavy fighting is expected to resume in the Kherson region.

story.headline: Iotova wins Bulgarian presidential runoff
story.summary: Incumbent Iliana Iotova won Bulgaria's 1 November presidential runoff with 57.5 percent.
story.display_body: Bulgaria's incumbent president, Iliana Iotova, won the presidential runoff on Sunday 1 November with 57.5% of the vote, according to the official count by the Central Election Commission. Her opponent, Andrey Gyurov, a former caretaker prime minister backed by the pro-Western liberal-conservative opposition, took 39.4% and accepted the result. Iotova is a former Socialist MEP who is seen as Russia-friendly and wants Ukraine and Russia to negotiate peace. She was backed by Prime Minister Rumen Radev's ruling Progressive Bulgaria party and the Socialists, and RFI's Sofia correspondent says the far-right also supported her. She becomes the first woman directly elected as Bulgaria's head of state. Drone attacks on ships near Bulgaria's Black Sea coast increased through October, and Radev and Iotova have avoided openly blaming Russia.
story.why: Bulgaria is an EU and NATO state on the Black Sea, and both its president and its government now favour talks with Moscow.

story.headline: Israeli forces leave Hebron after siege
story.summary: Israeli forces withdrew from Hebron after a ten-day siege launched after two soldiers were killed.
story.display_body: Israeli forces withdrew from Hebron in the occupied West Bank early on Monday 2 November, ending a ten-day siege of the city. The operation began on 23 October after two Israeli soldiers were shot dead near the city; Israeli forces later killed the two suspects. Hebron's governor, Khaled Dudin, said Palestinian security forces had "taken full control" of the area. The mayor said the city was told of the withdrawal at 06:00 local time, and that five universities had been closed and all movement in and out of the city stopped during the siege. An Israeli military official said about 3,000 Palestinians had been displaced and that the operation seized "four weapons and several bulletproof vests".
story.why: for ten days, one of the West Bank's largest cities was shut down in response to a single deadly attack.

story.headline: Sudan accuses Ethiopia at UN over drones
story.summary: Sudan filed complaints with the UN Security Council and AU accusing Ethiopia of letting the RSF launch drone attacks from its territory.
story.display_body: Sudan lodged complaints against Ethiopia with the UN Security Council and the African Union's Peace and Security Council on Sunday 1 November, accusing it of letting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) launch drones from Ethiopian territory. A report from Sudan's army-led Sovereignty Council lists 70 attacks between 15 February and 27 October involving 187 one-way attack drones (drones that crash into their target and explode). It says the attacks killed or wounded 484 civilians and killed 176 soldiers, and names Asosa airport, the Kurmuk–Gizen border area and the Bahir Dar air base as launch sites. Among them, it says, was a 9 October strike in Blue Nile state that killed 30 displaced women and children. Ethiopia accuses Sudan's army of backing Tigrayan rebels; Khartoum denies this. These are claims by one side in the war and have not been independently verified.
story.why: if the charge holds, Sudan's civil war, now in its fourth year, is spreading across a border into a regional conflict.

story.headline: Judge rejects Trump suit over Alaska count
story.summary: A federal judge rejected the Trump administration's pre-emptive suit to block certification of Alaska's Senate result.
story.display_body: A US federal judge has thrown out the Trump administration's pre-emptive lawsuit to stop Alaska certifying its Senate result if the Democratic candidate wins, ahead of the midterm vote on Tuesday 3 November. The administration argued that voters could confuse Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan with a newcomer on the same ballot, Dan J. Sullivan. Both face Democrat Mary Peltola. The court said the government had not explained how any mix-up could be identified without breaking the secrecy of the ballot. The Justice Department said it would challenge the ruling, but Senator Sullivan told CNN he would accept the result.
story.why: the administration tried to block the certification of a possible Republican defeat before polling day had even arrived. Tuesday's elections decide control of Congress, where Republicans hold very thin majorities.

story.headline: Impunity for journalist killings rises
story.summary: UNESCO reports 86 percent impunity for journalist killings in 2024-2025, the first rise since 2012, with 189 media workers killed.
story.display_body: About 86% of journalist killings went unpunished in 2024–2025, and 189 journalists and media workers were killed, UNESCO reported on Monday 2 November. It is the first rise in the impunity rate since UNESCO began measuring it in 2012, and the most deaths in any two-year period since 2014–2015. The Director-General's biennial report says 127 of the deaths (67%) were in conflict zones, the most in the Arab States (97). It names drones as a new threat to reporters at the front. UN Secretary-General António Guterres put impunity in conflict settings at "close to 100 per cent". The report is published for the International Day to End Impunity for Crimes against Journalists.
story.why: when killing a journalist almost never leads to a conviction, there is little to stop the next one, and news from war zones becomes thinner and less reliable.

story.headline: ELN camp strike toll rises to 19
story.summary: At least 19 bodies were counted after Venezuela's 30 October strike on an ELN camp, which a Venezuelan officer said had US support.
story.display_body: At least 19 bodies have now been counted from the Venezuelan army's 30 October bombing of an ELN guerrilla camp in Apure state. A senior Venezuelan officer told AFP the strike was carried out with US help. Yesterday's count from the NGO Fundaredes was nine. Fundaredes and local residents say 19 bodies were taken to the state capital, San Fernando. The officer, speaking anonymously, said drones and helicopters bombed the camp near Buena Vista del Meta at dawn, that "people from the CIA and FBI helped us. It was an order from the United States", and that the attack had been planned for a month. He said most of the dead were Venezuelan and that two were Dominican. Caracas has not commented, and the claim of US involvement is unconfirmed.
story.why: if Washington did help, Caracas has begun fighting Colombian guerrilla groups on its own soil with US support, after years in which Bogotá accused it of sheltering them.

story.headline: Swiss reservoirs at record autumn low
story.summary: Swiss hydro reservoirs were 74.1 percent full at end-September, the lowest for the date in the federal series, as gas and power prices rise.
story.display_body: Swiss hydro reservoirs were 74.1% full on 28 September, the lowest level for that point in the year in the Federal Office of Energy's series going back to 2000, and NZZ reports they had fallen to 70% by 26 October. At the end of September the reservoirs normally hold about 82–90%. The Federal Office of Energy's (BFE) open data puts stored energy at 6,588 GWh out of 8,895 GWh capacity. NZZ, citing the federal energy dashboard, says the 26 October figure is the lowest for the date since records began in 1997. Prices are rising too. European gas for next-month delivery has gone from about €72 per megawatt-hour in early October to over €100 at times, close to its autumn-2022 crisis level. On the Swiss forward market, power for delivery in 2027 rose 13% in two weeks. Gas storage in north-western Europe is about 23 percentage points below its long-term average, because suppliers held off refilling in the summer when the Iran war pushed prices up. The authorities say electricity or gas shortages remain unlikely, but traders are watching forecasts of what Axpo says could be one of the coldest Novembers in a decade.
story.why: Switzerland relies on stored hydropower and imports to get through the winter. Low reservoirs and dearer gas mean higher 2027 electricity tariffs are likely even if there are no shortages.

fields.display_body: Swiss hydro reservoirs were 74.1% full on 28 September, the lowest level for that point in the year in the Federal Office of Energy's series going back to 2000, and NZZ reports they had fallen to 70% by 26 October. At the end of September the reservoirs normally hold about 82–90%. The Federal Office of Energy's (BFE) open data puts stored energy at 6,588 GWh out of 8,895 GWh capacity. NZZ, citing the federal energy dashboard, says the 26 October figure is the lowest for the date since records began in 1997. Prices are rising too. European gas for next-month delivery has gone from about €72 per megawatt-hour in early October to over €100 at times, close to its autumn-2022 crisis level. On the Swiss forward market, power for delivery in 2027 rose 13% in two weeks. Gas storage in north-western Europe is about 23 percentage points below its long-term average, because suppliers held off refilling in the summer when the Iran war pushed prices up. The authorities say electricity or gas shortages remain unlikely, but traders are watching forecasts of what Axpo says could be one of the coldest Novembers in a decade.

story.headline: SRG radio returns to FM
story.summary: SRG will reactivate FM transmitters from mid-November 2026, covering about 80 percent of the population.
story.display_body: SRG, the Swiss public broadcaster, will start broadcasting its main radio channels on FM (UKW) again from mid-November 2026, almost two years after switching it off at the end of 2024. The Federal Office of Communications (BAKOM) granted the licence, which is now final because the appeal period has passed. The first transmitters will reach about 80% of the population, in all language regions, both at home and on the move. Programmes include the main channels, the SRF, RTS and RSI culture stations and SRF's regional news programmes in German-speaking Switzerland. The return costs about 6.5 million francs a year, which SRG must cover within the savings programme ordered by the Federal Council; full coverage used to cost about 15 million a year. Parliament voted in December 2025 to keep FM going beyond 2026, and SRG says it is now following that political decision.
story.why: listeners who lost SRG stations when FM was switched off, many of them older people or listening in cars, get them back without buying a DAB+ radio, and get more time to switch to digital.

story.headline: Cassis sets OSCE Lugano priorities
story.summary: Ignazio Cassis presented priorities for the OSCE ministerial council in Lugano on 3-4 December 2026.
story.display_body: Federal Councillor Ignazio Cassis, Switzerland's foreign minister and this year's OSCE chair, set out on Monday 2 November his priorities for the OSCE ministerial council in Lugano on 3–4 December 2026. Delegations from the 57 member states, including Russia, the US and Ukraine, and 12 partner countries are expected. At a news conference in Bellinzona with officials from the federal government, canton Ticino and the city of Lugano, Cassis said that "in a climate of growing instability… dialogue and diplomacy remain indispensable". The meeting closes the Swiss chairmanship year.
